title: How to Buy Aerogel Samples: Sample Costs, MOQs, and the Trial-to-Production Workflow
excerpt: How to request and evaluate aerogel samples before committing to volume: typical sample sizes and costs, minimum order quantities, three sourcing channels including China factory-direct, and the checks that separate real material from marketing claims.
content:
Buying an aerogel sample before committing to volume is the cheapest form of risk control in this industry. A 1 kg blanket sample and a few hundred dollars of third-party testing will tell you more about a supplier than any datasheet, trade show booth, or sales call. This guide covers what to ask for, what samples cost across the three main sourcing channels, and how to evaluate what arrives.

Why sample-first sourcing matters for aerogel

Aerogel blanket is a composite: silica aerogel loaded into a fiber matrix. Two products sold under the same name can differ in aerogel loading, density, hydrophobic treatment, and aging behavior, and the visible differences are small. Price spreads of 2–3x between suppliers quoting "the same" 10 mm hydrophobic blanket are routine. The only reliable way to know which quote represents real material is to hold and test the physical product.

For context on what drives those price differences, see the aerogel insulation price guide; this article covers the sample stage that precedes any volume decision.

What to specify when requesting a sample

A vague sample request gets a showroom piece. A precise request gets production-line material, which is what you actually need. Include these six items in every sample request:

  • Product and format. Blanket thickness and density (e.g., 10 mm, 200 kg/m³), particle size range for granules, or panel dimensions.
  • Quantity. Enough for your evaluation plus retention: typically 1–2 linear meters of blanket or 0.5–1 kg of granules.
  • Production lot. State that the sample must come from current production stock, not a specially prepared showcase batch.
  • Documentation. Datasheet, SDS, and — for factory-direct sourcing — a mill certificate or lot test report matching the sample.
  • Condition. Standard packaging, so you can also evaluate how the material survives handling.
  • Destination and timeline. Full delivery address with courier account number if you want to control freight.

Factory-direct samples from China

Most Chinese aerogel producers sell samples routinely, because sample-first evaluation is the norm for industrial insulation sourcing. Expect per-kilogram sample pricing above bulk rates — commonly USD 8–15 per kg for blanket cut pieces against USD 3–8 per kg at container volume — or a flat sample fee in the USD 20–150 range for a sheet plus documentation. Many factories waive the material charge when the buyer provides a courier account number (DHL/FedEx/UPS collect), which keeps the factory's cost near zero. Sample air freight for a 1–2 kg parcel from China typically costs USD 40–120.

When screening candidates, the China aerogel supplier directory and the China supplier directory on aerogela are structured starting points. Verify business licenses and export history before wiring any payment.

Distributor and local samples

Distributors price samples higher but deliver faster and in smaller increments — often a single A4 sheet of blanket. For projects in North America or Europe, this is the fastest path to a physical evaluation, and it tests the channel you would actually buy volume through if specification names a certified system.

Research-grade small quantities

For laboratory work, aerogel powders and monolithic pieces are sold by specialist suppliers and marketplaces at USD 50–500+ per sample unit. Quantities are small (grams to hundreds of grams) and the material is often TEOS-based rather than the water-glass chemistry used in industrial blanket, so results from research-grade material do not transfer directly to industrial product evaluation.

How to evaluate the sample when it arrives

Run a structured evaluation, and keep the unsampled remainder as retention. A practical in-house sequence:

  1. Physical inspection. Measure actual thickness and areal density against the datasheet. Density off by more than 10% from spec means either poor process control or a different product than quoted.
  2. Handling check. Flex the blanket sample. Excessive dusting (aerogel powder shedding) indicates weak fiber-matrix bonding or low aerogel loading; some dust is normal, a cloud of it is not.
  3. Moisture test. Drop water on the surface. Hydrophobic blanket should bead water with no darkening wick into the material.
  4. Comparative insulation test. A simple side-by-side hot-plate or guarded comparison against your incumbent insulation at equal thickness tells you whether the claimed conductivity advantage is real at your conditions.
  5. Third-party verification (recommended for volume decisions). Send a portion to an accredited lab for thermal conductivity (ASTM C177 or ISO 8301), density, and hydrophobicity. A few hundred dollars here protects five- and six-figure material orders.

Match every test result against the lot test report the supplier sent with the sample. Consistent, documented results from a named production lot are the signal you are looking for.

Red flags during the sample stage

  • Refusal to state the production lot or provide a lot-matched test report
  • Sample noticeably better than what the same supplier's references describe (showcase material)
  • Quotes that shift between USD/kg and USD/m² without stating density and thickness
  • Datasheet conductivity quoted without a reference temperature or test standard
  • Payment demanded exclusively through channels without commercial traceability

Any one of these is a reason to widen your sample set to other suppliers rather than proceed.

From sample to production order

A passing sample converts to a production order through a trial lot: typically one pallet to a partial container, priced between sample and full bulk rates, with the same lot-traceability documentation you evaluated on the sample. State in writing that the trial lot must match the evaluated sample in density, conductivity, and hydrophobicity, and re-verify on arrival with the same in-house checks. Only after a successful trial lot does container-volume pricing and the 3–8 USD/kg factory-direct range discussed in the price guide become a realistic target.

FAQ

Where can I buy aerogel samples?

Three channels: direct from producers (including Chinese factories, most of which sell samples routinely), from Western distributors for fast domestic delivery, and from research suppliers or marketplaces for laboratory quantities of powder, granules, or monolithic material.

How much does an aerogel sample cost?

Blanket samples typically cost USD 20–150 direct from Chinese factories (sometimes free against a courier account), USD 50–300 from Western distributors, and USD 50–500+ for research-grade small quantities. Add USD 40–120 for international air freight of a 1–2 kg parcel.

What is the minimum order quantity for aerogel?

Samples are usually 1–2 blanket meters or 0.5–1 kg of granules. Trial lots commonly start at one pallet; factory-direct bulk pricing generally begins at container-load volume. Below those thresholds, expect per-kilogram pricing 2–4x above container rates.

Can I get a free aerogel sample from China?

Many Chinese producers waive the material charge when you provide a courier account number, because it costs them little to prepare. Treat genuinely free samples as an evaluation convenience, not a signal of supplier quality — verification effort stays the same.

What tests should I run on an aerogel sample?

At minimum: thickness and density verification against the datasheet, a flex and dusting check, and a water-drop hydrophobicity test. Before volume commitments, add third-party thermal conductivity (ASTM C177 / ISO 8301) and hydrophobicity testing at an accredited lab.

How long does it take to get an aerogel sample from China?

Typically 5–15 days door to door by air courier. Factory preparation takes 1–5 days; the balance is air transit and customs. Distributor samples within Europe or North America usually arrive in 2–7 days.
